title: Two Workers Pulled Alive From Nepal Tunnel Nine Days After Devastating Floods
excerpt: Sanjay Sah and Kabir Maharjan are the first survivors rescued from hydropower tunnels where hundreds remain trapped after the August 26 glacier collapse.
body:
• Sanjay Sah and Kabir Maharjan were pulled alive from the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station tunnel on Friday, nine days after a glacier collapse sent a wall of ice, rock, and mud through the valley.
  • Sah, a mechanical foreman, stayed behind in the control room to help colleagues escape and spent nine days reciting mantras in darkness; he says three or four others may still be alive deeper in the tunnel.
  • At least 1,287 people have been killed and more than 5,080 remain missing across Nepal, with flood losses estimated at $2.56 billion.
  • Officials believe around 900 workers are trapped in tunnels linked to six hydropower projects along the Trishuli River.

Rescuers pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel on Nepal's Trishuli River on Friday, nine days after a glacier collapse triggered catastrophic floods that have killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing across the Himalayan nation.

Sanjay Sah, a 30-year-old mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor, were brought out of the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station — the first survivors rescued from the hydropower projects devastated by the August 26 disaster, according to Reuters.

A Choice to Stay

When word reached the control room that a wall of debris was barreling down the valley, Sah urged his colleagues to flee. He stayed behind.

"I was in the control room, so my responsibility was to save everyone's lives. When there was such a big accident, it was not right for me to run away."

— Sanjay Sah, mechanical foreman, Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station

By the time Sah turned to run, there was no time left. For nine days he sat in the tunnel's darkness, chanting mantras to hold onto hope. He told rescuers he had been in contact with three or four other workers somewhere in the tunnel and said others could still be trapped deeper into the mountain.

Videos released by Nepali authorities showed Maharjan being hoisted from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered, then lowered onto a stretcher. Sah was carried out on a worker's back, his face still caked in mud, before army doctors fitted an oxygen mask and checked his vitals inside a rescue tent.

Scale of the Disaster

At least 1,287 people have been killed in Nepal since the August 26 glacier collapse sent a surge of ice, rock, and mud crashing through the Trishuli valley, sweeping away houses, streets, and schools in towns and villages near the border with China's Tibet, according to Nepal's disaster management authority. More than 5,080 people remain missing. China has put the death toll in Tibet at 21, with 541 others listed as missing.

Officials believe at least 900 workers are trapped in tunnels connected to six hydropower projects along the river. At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A project alone, including about 115 believed to be trapped in its main tunnel, according to The Times.

Nepal's army called the rescue the "rebirth of two lives." Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said 75 army troops and 18 paramilitary personnel were involved in the operation, which included controlled explosions and excavators clearing mud and debris at depths of about 30 feet, according to the Wall Street Journal.

A $2.56 Billion Toll

Property, housing, and infrastructure worth at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion) was destroyed in the disaster, according to Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Nepal will need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, with at least 7,500 homes completely destroyed.

Commercial insurance losses could exceed $132.3 million, with hydropower projects accounting for most claims, according to a top official at one of the country's leading insurers. At least 583 foreign nationals — many of them pilgrims and trekkers — remain missing.

Search Operations Continue

Both survivors are now in intensive care at an army hospital in Kathmandu with stable vital signs. Maharjan cannot move his hands or legs, but Sah's injuries are not considered critical, according to an aide to Nepal's energy minister.

"I have been hearing from the news that my brother has been found. The entire family is very happy."

— Amir Maharjan, brother of rescued worker Kabir Maharjan

A team of engineers in a WhatsApp group has been guiding rescue workers at the hydropower sites, providing technical knowledge about tunnel layouts alongside helicopters and heavy machinery. Rescue teams from India, South Korea, China, and Australia have joined the search for survivors. Officials at the Trishuli 3A site believe some of the workers still inside the tunnel could be alive, and rescue operations were continuing Friday.

nri_angle: India has sent rescue experts to assist Nepal's search operations, and hundreds of foreign nationals including pilgrims and trekkers remain missing.
